questions.stem: Which resource of Attica did most to pay for the Athenian fleet and the city's coinage?
options: The gold mines of Mount Pentelikon
The copper deposits of Mount Hymettus
The iron ore of the Thriasian plain
The silver mines at Laurion
questions.explanation: Silver from Laurion in southern Attica was minted into Athenian coins and, from the 480s, helped build the fleet. Mount Pentelikon supplied marble, not gold, and Hymettus was known for honey and stone.

questions.stem: Attica's thin, stony soils grew olives and vines well but not enough grain for its people. What was the main consequence for Athens?
options: It banned the export of olive oil so that farmers would switch to grain
It moved most of its citizens to cleruchies in the fertile Nile Delta
It relied on grain sent each year as a gift from the kings of Persia
It depended on imported grain, much of it shipped from the Black Sea
questions.explanation: Athens imported grain by sea, especially from the Black Sea region, so control of the sea routes and the Hellespont was vital. This is one reason the navy mattered so much to the city.

questions.stem: The marble used for the Parthenon was quarried mainly from:
options: Mount Pentelikon in Attica
the island of Paros
Mount Hymettus near the city
the hills above Laurion
questions.explanation: Pentelic marble, from Mount Pentelikon north-east of Athens, was used for the Parthenon and other Periclean buildings. Parian marble was prized for sculpture but was not the main stone of the Parthenon.

questions.stem: In the 450s BCE the Athenians built the Long Walls. What did these walls achieve?
options: They separated the citizens' quarter of the city from the quarter of the metics
They protected the silver mines at Laurion from raids by the slaves working there
They joined the city to its port, so Athens could be supplied by sea in a siege
They enclosed all of Attica, so farmers could stay on their land in wartime
questions.explanation: The Long Walls ran from Athens to the coast, making the city and the Piraeus one fortress. As long as Athens ruled the sea, it could not be starved out by a land army, though the countryside lay open to attack.

questions.stem: The 'Old Oligarch', an anonymous fifth-century pamphlet on the Athenian constitution, argues that it is fair for the poor to have power because they row the fleet. Why is this source especially useful?
options: It is a contemporary view by a critic who still explains how the democracy worked
It was written by Pericles himself to defend his own reforms before the Athenian assembly
It is an official record of the decrees passed by the Athenian assembly
It was written by a Spartan visitor with no reason to favour either side
questions.explanation: The author dislikes democracy but explains why it works in its own terms, linking the power of the poor to the navy. As a hostile contemporary he gives a view different from both Thucydides and the later Plutarch.

questions.stem: Each year one-sixtieth of the allies' tribute was given to Athena, and the amounts were inscribed on stone. What can historians learn from these Athenian Tribute Lists?
options: Why each allied city chose to stay in the league rather than revolt
Which cities paid and roughly how much, which helps track the empire over time
The full text of the speeches made by Pericles in support of the empire
The exact number of Athenian citizens and metics who rowed in the fleet in each year
questions.explanation: Because the first-fruits to Athena were recorded city by city, scholars can work out who paid and estimate the tribute. The lists are damaged and say nothing about motives or speeches.

questions.stem: Most written sources on Periclean Athens were produced by educated citizen men, many of them hostile to or proud of the democracy. What is the main problem this creates?
options: The sources describe only Sparta and must be applied to Athens
Women, metics and slaves are seen mostly through the eyes of others
No written source from the fifth century BCE survives at all
All the sources were written in Latin long after the events
questions.explanation: Thucydides, the dramatists and the Old Oligarch survive, but they reflect the outlook of elite citizen men. The lives of women, metics and enslaved people must be pieced together from their remarks, inscriptions, vase painting and archaeology.

questions.stem: Plays and texts suggest that respectable Athenian women stayed indoors, yet vase paintings and religious duties show women at fountains, festivals and funerals. How do many modern historians resolve this?
options: Women's lives cannot be studied, because no source mentions them at all
Seclusion was an elite ideal; poorer women worked outside and all had religious roles
The written texts are reliable and the vase paintings show only foreign women
Athenian women had the same public and political rights as men, so the written texts are satire
questions.explanation: Many scholars see strict seclusion as an ideal of wealthy families: poorer women sold goods and fetched water, and citizen women of all classes had vital roles in cult. The evidence is therefore read as showing ideals and practice side by side.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that Athenian democracy was made possible by slavery and by the empire's tribute. Which evidence would best support this view?
options: Generals were elected by show of hands rather than chosen by lot
Tribute and slave labour freed citizens' time and funded pay for public service
The Funeral Oration says that Athens was open to the whole world and never expelled foreigners
Athenian women took part in the Panathenaic procession each year
questions.explanation: Pay for jurors and rowers and the building program drew on imperial revenue, and slaves worked mines, farms and workshops, giving citizens time for politics. Critics of the view stress that most citizens were small farmers who worked their own land.

questions.stem: In Athenian political language, the demos was:
options: the citizen body as a whole, especially as it met to decide
the council of former archons that met on the hill of the Areopagus
the board of ten generals elected each year by the tribes
the class of wealthy landowners who served as cavalry
questions.explanation: Demos meant the people: the whole body of citizens, and in practice the ordinary citizens who outnumbered the rich. Democracy (demokratia) was rule by the demos.

questions.stem: A polis such as Athens was more than its town. Which statement best describes it?
options: A temple estate run by priests on behalf of the city's patron god
A trading post founded and ruled by merchants from overseas
A community of citizens with its own territory, laws, gods and army
A town governed by officials appointed by a distant Greek king
questions.explanation: The Athenian polis included the city, the Piraeus and all of Attica, with its citizens, laws, cults and armed forces. It was self-governing, not ruled from outside.

questions.stem: In 457/6 BCE the archonship was opened to the zeugitai. Which class had been allowed to hold it before this change?
options: Only the thetes and the zeugitai
All four property classes equally
Only the hippeis and the zeugitai
Only the pentakosiomedimnoi and the hippeis
questions.explanation: The two richest classes, the pentakosiomedimnoi and hippeis, alone had been eligible. Admitting the zeugitai, the middling farmers who served as hoplites, widened access to the office.

questions.stem: The thetes, the lowest of the four property classes, mattered greatly to Periclean Athens because they:
options: supplied the cavalry that guarded the frontiers of Attica
paid most of the city's direct taxes each year
filled the priesthoods of the major city cults
provided most of the rowers who crewed the fleet
questions.explanation: The thetes owned too little to arm themselves as hoplites, but they rowed the triremes on which Athenian power rested. Their service strengthened their claim to a full voice in the assembly.

questions.stem: Cephalus, a wealthy Syracusan whose family owned a shield workshop, lived in the Piraeus for decades but was never a citizen. As a metic he would have:
options: gained the right to vote in the assembly once he had lived in Athens for ten years
been treated in law as the property of his citizen sponsor
paid the metic tax and had a citizen sponsor, but could not own land in Attica
been free of all taxes and military service in return for his skills
questions.explanation: Metics paid an annual tax, the metoikion, needed a citizen prostates and could not own land or houses without a special grant. They served in the army and navy and paid special levies, but had no political rights.

questions.stem: Enslaved people in Periclean Athens were most likely to be found:
options: in households, workshops, farms and, in harsh conditions, the silver mines
only in the silver mines, since the law banned slaves in the city itself
mainly as soldiers, forming the core of the hoplite phalanx
only in the service of the state, since private slavery was forbidden
questions.explanation: Slaves did domestic work, laboured in craft workshops and on farms, and worked the Laurion mines in the worst conditions. Some were owned by the state, but private ownership was common.

questions.stem: The Old Oligarch complains that in Athens you cannot tell slaves and metics from citizens by their dress, and that slaves are not struck in the street. What is the best way to use this complaint?
options: As a hostile view that hints slaves were visible in public life, not proof they were well treated
As proof that slavery had been abolished in Athens by the time of Pericles
As evidence that metics and slaves held the same rights as citizens
As official law, since the Old Oligarch was a magistrate recording statutes
questions.explanation: The writer is complaining about democracy, so he exaggerates its leniency. The remark suggests slaves mixed freely in the streets, but it says nothing reliable about their conditions in the mines or households.

questions.stem: In Athenian law, a citizen woman was under the legal guardianship of a male relative called her:
options: prostates
strategos
epistates
kyrios
questions.explanation: The kyrios, usually her father, then her husband, acted for a woman in law and in property matters. A prostates was the citizen sponsor of a metic, and an epistates presided over the council for a day.

questions.stem: After Pericles' citizenship law of 451/0 BCE, a citizen woman's status became more important because:
options: citizen women were now able to marry metics and keep their status
a man's children were citizens only if both parents were Athenian
women gained the right to vote in the assembly through their sons
only women could pass on land to their children under the new law
questions.explanation: The law limited citizenship to children of an Athenian father and an Athenian mother, so a wife's descent decided her children's rights. It did not give women any political vote.

questions.stem: An epikleros was an Athenian woman whose father died leaving no sons. What usually happened to her?
options: She was married to her nearest male relative, to keep the property in the family
She inherited the estate in her own name and managed it without a guardian
She was dedicated as a priestess of Athena and her property went to the temple
Her father's estate passed to the state, and she received a small pension
questions.explanation: The epikleros went with the estate to her closest male kin, such as her father's brother, so that the property and the household line continued. She did not own it in her own right.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Athenian boule in the time of Pericles is correct?
options: Its 300 members were former archons who served on the Areopagus
Its 600 members were nominated by the generals at the start of each war
Its 500 members were chosen by lot, fifty from each tribe, for one year
Its 500 members were elected for life by the assembly from the richest class
questions.explanation: The council was chosen by lot from citizens over thirty, fifty from each of the ten tribes, serving for a year. It prepared business for the assembly and oversaw officials.

questions.stem: During its prytany, each tribe's group of fifty councillors had a special role. What was it?
options: They chose the archons and generals for the following year by lot
They acted as a standing committee, dining in the Tholos and calling meetings
They commanded the fleet and chose which of the allied cities to attack that year
They served as the jury for every case heard in the courts that month
questions.explanation: The prytaneis ran daily business for a tenth of the year, dined in the Tholos and summoned the council and assembly. One of them, chosen by lot, was epistates for a day and a night.

questions.stem: Before the ekklesia voted on a matter, the boule normally prepared a proposal called a probouleuma. What does this show about the two bodies?
options: The council could veto any decision of the assembly that it disliked
The assembly only advised, and the council made the binding decisions
The two bodies met together as a single chamber for every vote
The council prepared business, but the assembly made the final decision
questions.explanation: Probouleusis meant the council set the agenda and drafted motions, but the assembly debated, amended and voted. Power rested with the citizen body meeting on the Pnyx.

questions.stem: The Athenian ekklesia met on a hillside near the Agora called the:
options: Areopagus
Acropolis
Kerameikos
Pnyx
questions.explanation: The assembly met on the Pnyx, where any adult male citizen could attend, speak and vote. The Areopagus was the hill of the old aristocratic council.

questions.stem: Most Athenian officials were chosen by lot, but the ten strategoi were elected by show of hands and could be re-elected every year. What best explains the difference?
options: Command in war needed proven skill, so the citizens chose for ability
The generals were priests, so the gods had to approve them by an omen
Only the richest class could vote, so they kept the office for themselves
Lot had not yet been invented, so all offices were filled by election
questions.explanation: Athenians accepted lot for routine offices but wanted experienced men leading armies and fleets. Election and unlimited re-election are why ambitious leaders such as Pericles held power through the generalship.

questions.stem: An Athenian jury in the heliaea typically:
options: numbered hundreds of citizens over thirty, voting without a judge to guide them
had twelve members chosen by lot, guided by a professional judge appointed for life
was made up of the five ephors, who heard every case in the city
consisted of the ten generals, who judged all crimes against the state
questions.explanation: Jurors came from an annual panel of 6,000 citizens over thirty, and courts were large, often several hundred. There were no professional judges or lawyers: litigants spoke for themselves and the jury voted at once.

questions.stem: A trierarch in Periclean Athens was:
options: the admiral appointed by Sparta to command the allied fleets
a metic shipbuilder who held the state contract for building all of the city's triremes
a wealthy citizen who paid to maintain and command a trireme for a year
a thete elected by his fellow rowers to lead them in the assembly
questions.explanation: The trierarchy was a liturgy, a public service imposed on the rich: the state supplied the hull and crew pay, and the trierarch fitted it out and commanded it. Each trireme needed about 170 rowers, so the system tied the wealthy to the naval power that empowered the poor.

questions.stem: Which combination of functions best describes the Athenian Agora?
options: The naval harbour where the triremes were built and stored
The cemetery outside the walls where citizens were buried
Market, meeting place, home of the council and law courts, and setting for festivals
A fortified citadel on a rocky hill, holding the city's main temples and the treasury
questions.explanation: The Agora held shops and stalls, the Bouleuterion and Tholos, stoas such as the Painted Stoa, courts and shrines, and the Panathenaic Way crossed it. The Acropolis was the citadel and the Kerameikos the cemetery.

questions.stem: The Piraeus was laid out on a regular grid plan and had three harbours: Kantharos for trade, and Zea and Mounichia with shipsheds. Its significance to Athens was that it was:
options: a sacred site where only priests and their slaves were allowed to live
a separate polis that paid tribute to Athens as a member of the league
a small fishing village of no importance until the Roman period
the base of the fleet and the hub of the trade that fed the city
questions.explanation: The Piraeus was both the navy's base and the commercial port, home to many metics and traders. Grain imports, harbour dues and the fleet all centred there.

questions.stem: In 454/3 BCE the treasury of the Delian League was moved from Delos to Athens. What was a major result of this move?
options: The allies gained full control of the fund and chose how it was spent
The tribute was abolished and replaced by contributions of ships
Sparta took over leadership of the league and its funds
Athens could draw on the allies' tribute for its own purposes, including building
questions.explanation: With the treasury in Athens, tribute was in Athenian hands, and some of it funded the fleet and the building program on the Acropolis. Critics in Athens and among the allies saw this as turning an alliance into an empire.

questions.stem: A cleruchy was:
options: a settlement of Athenian citizens on land taken from an allied or conquered state
a fortified Spartan garrison placed by Sparta in an allied city that had revolted from Athens
a tax paid by metics in return for the right to live in Attica
a court that heard disputes between Athens and its allied cities
questions.explanation: Cleruchs kept their Athenian citizenship while farming land overseas, which helped poorer Athenians and served as a garrison over the allies. Cleruchies were resented by the allies who lost land.

questions.stem: Athenian silver coins, widely used across the Greek world, showed:
options: the Parthenon on one side and an olive branch on the other
the head of Athena on one side and an owl on the other
the head of Pericles on one side and a trireme on the other
the god Poseidon on one side and a trident on the other
questions.explanation: The 'owls' carried Athena's head and her owl, with the letters of the city's name. Living men such as Pericles did not appear on Athenian coins.

questions.stem: The building accounts of the Erechtheion, begun after Pericles' death, list citizens, metics and slaves working side by side at similar rates. What does this suggest about crafts in Athens?
options: Only slaves were allowed to work as builders and sculptors in Athens
Citizens refused all manual work, leaving crafts entirely to metics
Metics were barred from public building contracts by law
Skilled work was done by all three groups, and status did not fix the job
questions.explanation: The accounts show a mixed workforce, often paid a drachma a day whatever their status. They date from the end of the century, so they illustrate craft work in Periclean Athens rather than describe it directly.

questions.stem: Athena Parthenos, the great gold and ivory statue in the Parthenon, was made by:
options: Myron
Phidias
Polykleitos
Praxiteles
questions.explanation: Phidias made the Athena Parthenos and, according to Plutarch, oversaw the whole building program. Polykleitos worked mainly in Argos, and Praxiteles belongs to the fourth century.

questions.stem: In fifth-century Athens, priests and priestesses were usually:
options: a full-time professional class trained in the temples and kept separate from ordinary citizens
foreign experts brought from Egypt to perform the city's sacrifices
elected by the assembly to interpret sacred books of doctrine
citizens who served a particular god's cult, some from old families and some by lot
questions.explanation: Greek priesthoods belonged to particular cults: the priestess of Athena Polias came from an old family, while the new priestess of Athena Nike was chosen by lot from all Athenian women. They led sacrifices and cared for sanctuaries; there was no sacred book or separate clergy.

questions.stem: At the Great Dionysia, before the plays began, the allies' tribute was displayed in the theatre and the sons of citizens killed in war paraded in armour. What does this reveal about the festival?
options: Only allies and foreigners attended, since citizens were barred from the theatre
The festival honoured Athena alone and had nothing to do with Dionysus
Drama festivals also celebrated the power and values of the Athenian state
The festival was a private event paid for by the families of dead soldiers
questions.explanation: The Great Dionysia honoured Dionysus, but its ceremonies also displayed Athenian wealth, empire and civic duty to citizens and visitors. Drama was funded through the choregia, a liturgy on wealthy citizens.

questions.stem: The Thesmophoria was a festival of Demeter that:
options: was held every four years with athletic and musical games for men
was celebrated by married citizen women, with men excluded
was celebrated by boys completing their military training
featured contests of tragedy and comedy in the theatre
questions.explanation: The Thesmophoria was for citizen wives, who camped together and performed rites for Demeter linked to fertility and the harvest. Aristophanes later made a comedy about a man who sneaks in.

questions.stem: Thucydides describes the public funeral for Athenians killed in war: their bones were placed in ten cypress coffins, one for each tribe, with an empty bier for the missing, and a leading citizen gave a speech. What does this custom show?
options: The polis honoured its dead collectively, as citizens rather than as family heroes
Families were forbidden to mourn soldiers, who belonged only to the gods
Only the generals who died in battle were given any form of burial
War dead were buried inside the Parthenon as offerings to Athena
questions.explanation: The state funeral grouped the dead by tribe and buried them together in the public cemetery, stressing equal service to the city. Private funerals, by contrast, involved the prothesis and ekphora carried out by the family.

questions.stem: In an Athenian private funeral, the prothesis was:
options: the laying out of the body at home for mourning
the procession carrying the body to the cemetery
the speech given in praise of the dead person
the meal held at the tomb on the anniversary
questions.explanation: The body was washed, dressed and laid out at home, where women led the lament. The ekphora was the procession to burial outside the city walls.

questions.stem: The Parthenon is built in the Doric order, yet a continuous carved frieze ran around its inner building, showing a great procession. Why is this frieze notable?
options: A continuous frieze is an Ionic feature, combined here with a Doric temple
It is the only part of the temple to be made of wood rather than marble
It shows the Persian king and his satraps paying tribute to the Athenian assembly
It was painted on plaster rather than carved, so none of it survives
questions.explanation: The frieze, usually linked to a procession such as the Panathenaic, is an Ionic element set within a Doric building. Its subject and design make it a central source for Athenian religious ideals.

questions.stem: Sophocles produced tragedies at the Great Dionysia and also served as a general in the war against Samos. What does his career suggest about culture in Periclean Athens?
options: Writers were citizens active in public life, and drama was a civic institution
Playwrights were professional entertainers barred from holding public office
Tragedy was a private art enjoyed only by a small circle of aristocrats
Generals were expected to write plays as part of their official duties
questions.explanation: Tragedians competed in state festivals before thousands of citizens and could hold office like any other citizen. Drama explored questions of law, gods and the city in a public setting.
